title: The Red Pen That Never Comes Back

briefing.headline: Junior lawyers in a Belgian law firm: what you should know before the call
points: Young lawyers in Belgium do a three-year traineeship at the bar under a supervising lawyer, combined with compulsory courses organised by the bar.
Law firms bill clients by the hour; every lawyer records time, and partners decide which hours are actually billed and which are written off.
Most firms in Brussels work in Dutch, French and English, sometimes in the same file.
Partners usually run their own client relationships and teams, and decisions about the firm are taken by the partners together.

stakeholder.name: Geert Hendrickx
stakeholder.org: Hendrickx Lambrecht & Partners, a business law firm in Brussels with 14 partners and 22 junior associates
stakeholder.voice: Courteous, precise, slightly pompous. Uses Latin when nervous and calls the juniors 'our young colleagues'. Measures everything in hours and is quietly proud of his own drafting.

frontline.name: Sarah Peeters
frontline.role: Junior associate, corporate department, second year
frontline.voice: Bright, tired, ironic, careful not to sound ungrateful. Talks fast and checks the corridor before saying anything about a partner.

opening_message: Good afternoon. Our partners complain, unanimously for once, that our young colleagues cannot write. Memos, contract drafts, letters to clients: everything needs rewriting. I would like a writing training for all 22 junior associates. Legal writing, structure, concision. Preferably by someone with a reputation. In January, when the hours are calmer.
surface_ask: A legal writing course for all 22 junior associates.

gold.real_problem: Partners rewrite junior drafts themselves, often late at night, and almost never return them with comments, so juniors never learn what was wrong. Each partner wants a different structure and the firm has no house style. Juniors are judged on billable hours recorded, so rereading and restructuring a draft feels like time they cannot afford, and partners write off much of the drafting time anyway. The one department where a partner reviews drafts in short sit-downs has hardly any rewriting. The writing gap is real but small; the feedback and incentive system keeps it in place.
gold.need_statement: Juniors need regular, specific feedback on their own drafts and one agreed standard for what a good memo looks like; partners need a reason to give that feedback and juniors need permission to spend time on quality. A short writing module helps only if partners agree on the standard and review drafts with the junior.

hidden_facts.fact: Time records show 31% of junior drafting hours are written off across the firm: 44% in the corporate department, 12% in litigation.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what the rewriting costs, whether time records show it, or whether some departments have less of a problem.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Write-offs on drafting? I would have to look. ... 31% overall. Corporate 44. Litigation 12. Well. Litigation has simpler documents.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Junior associates, drafting hours recorded vs billed, last 12 months. Firm: 31% written off. Corporate: 44%. Tax: 33%. Employment: 28%. Litigation: 12%.

hidden_facts.fact: Partners rewrite drafts themselves and send the final version to the client. Juniors rarely get their draft back with comments; they often find out what changed only by comparing their version with what the client received.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what happens to a draft after a junior hands it in, or how juniors get feedback.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: What happens to the draft? The partner improves it. It goes to the client. ... Do they get it back? I suppose they can see the final version in the file.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: Feedback? I send a draft at eight. At two in the morning a partner sends the client something completely different. I find out what I did wrong by putting the two side by side. In Word. With the compare function. That's my mentor.

hidden_facts.fact: Each partner expects a different structure: one wants the conclusion first, one wants facts and law first in academic style, one wants bullet points, one wants English throughout. There is no house style or model memo, and juniors are told to 'just know' each partner's taste. Rereading a draft feels unaffordable because it isn't billable.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what a good memo looks like here, whether there is a house style, or how juniors decide how much time to spend on a draft.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: A house style? Every partner has his own standards. That's rather the charm of the profession.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: I work for four partners. One wants the answer in the first line. One wants three pages of facts before the answer. One wants bullets. One wants it in English even when the client is from Aalst. And rereading? If I reread it, I can't bill it, and if I bill it, he writes it off. So you send it and pray.

hidden_facts.fact: Juniors have a target of 1,800 billable hours a year. Their bonus is based on hours recorded, and non-billable time for know-how and training is capped at 50 hours.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how juniors are evaluated, about targets or bonuses, or how much time they have for learning.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Our young colleagues have an 1,800-hour target. Like everywhere. Training counts as non-billable, up to 50 hours. That's quite generous.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Junior associates: target 1,800 billable hours per year. Bonus: based on billable hours recorded against target. Non-billable allowance (know-how, internal training): maximum 50 hours per year. Feedback: annual evaluation by the supervising partner.

hidden_facts.fact: Anne Lambrecht, the litigation partner, reviews every junior draft in a 20-minute sit-down the same day. Her juniors' drafts rarely need rewriting. The other partners say she 'has time because litigation is slower'.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks whether any partner or department does it differently, or whether some juniors write better than others.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Anne sits with her juniors and goes through every draft. Twenty minutes. It's charming. She has the time; litigation is a slower rhythm.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: The litigation juniors are fine. Anne sits with them for twenty minutes and goes through the draft with a pen. We call it the confessional. They all want to be in it.

hidden_facts.fact: Five of the firm's last fourteen juniors left within their first two years; three said in exit talks that they 'never knew what they were doing wrong'.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks about turnover, why juniors leave, or what exit talks say.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Some leave, yes. That's the profession. Some go to in-house jobs. Better hours. Less... red.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Junior associates hired 2003-2005: 14. Left within two years: 5. Reasons given at exit talk: 'no feedback' or 'never knew what was wrong' (3), salary (1), relocation (1).

volunteered_facts: A one-day legal writing seminar with a law professor ran last year; the juniors rated it 4.6 out of 5.

constraints.budget: About 20,000 euro; the partners would rather pay for a well-known name than for 'consultants'.
constraints.deadline: January, before the annual evaluations in March.
constraints.audience: 22 junior associates in five departments; 14 partners, who decide everything together.
constraints.schedule: Juniors bill from early morning to late evening; anything during office hours eats into their target, anything after hours is resented.
constraints.languages: Dutch, French and English; the bar courses are in the junior's language of registration.
data_available: Time records with hours recorded and billed per lawyer
data_not_available: Any record of how many drafts were rewritten and why
Partner-level feedback data (no partner has ever been evaluated)

dependencies.concern: Any change to targets, write-offs or a house style needs agreement from 14 partners who each run their own way.
dependencies.if_ignored: The course runs and each partner keeps rewriting in his own style.

dependencies.concern: Her practice is the proof that review works, but she won't want to be held up as the example against her partners.
dependencies.if_ignored: The best internal model is never used.

dependencies.concern: Traineeship rules require a supervising lawyer to actually supervise, and bar courses already cover some writing.
dependencies.if_ignored: The course duplicates the bar's and nobody asks what supervision means.

dependencies.concern: Owns the billable targets and the 50-hour non-billable cap.
dependencies.if_ignored: Juniors have no time to apply anything they learn.

traps: Satisfaction with the course, which was already 4.6 last year.
Partners' general impression that 'writing has improved'.
Billable hours per junior, which rewards speed over quality.

gold_plan.baseline: Share of junior drafting hours written off, per department, over the last 12 months.
gold_plan.behaviour: Drafts returned to the junior with comments or a short review talk, logged on a sample of files.
gold_plan.leading_indicators: Number of drafts reviewed with the junior per month; drafts that go to the client with only minor changes.
gold_plan.business_metric: Write-offs on junior drafting hours and junior turnover within two years.
gold_plan.collection: Monthly write-off report from time records, a simple tick box in the file on whether the draft was reviewed, exit and annual talks.

concepts.conventional: A one- or two-day legal writing course for all 22 juniors, with a known professor.
concepts.solid: A short writing workshop using the juniors' own anonymised drafts, after the partners agree one model memo and house style. Partners return each draft with comments or a 15-minute review, with that review time recorded as non-billable training outside the 50-hour cap. Pilot in corporate, where write-offs are highest.
next_level_examples: Make Anne's 'confessional' the firm standard in one department, framed as recovering written-off hours rather than as being nice to juniors.
Put partners in the room: a session where partners mark the same draft separately, discover they disagree, and agree a house style on the spot.
Show the partners the write-off numbers in euros: what the evening rewriting costs them per year, against twenty minutes of review.
also_valid: A writing course for juniors is acceptable if it is built on a partner-agreed standard and followed by real draft reviews.
red_flags: A writing course alone as the answer.
Framing the juniors as poor writers without looking at feedback.
Ignoring the billable-hour target and the write-offs.

defence_objections: You want me to tell fourteen partners they need to change how they work? I have to have lunch with them. Every day.
Twenty minutes per draft, per junior, per partner? That's hours of non-billable time. Who pays for that?
A house style? My partners have been writing for thirty years. You'd have an easier time agreeing on the Pope.
question_you_didnt_ask: What happens to a draft after the junior hands it in?
actor_notes: Geert believes the problem is the juniors and that his own drafting is exemplary; he becomes defensive if partners are criticised directly.
He reveals the lack of feedback only when asked about what happens to a draft, and frames it as partners being generous with their evenings.
He dismisses Anne's approach until the player connects it to the write-off numbers; money moves him more than development.
His risk appetite is low: anything that needs a partners' meeting vote triggers a defence round. A pilot in one department is the move he can accept.
flavour_lines: Our young colleagues have excellent degrees. They write like their thesis supervisors. That's the problem.
I correct drafts at night. It's very relaxing. My wife disagrees.
